blocks.content: Have you ever tried to add one new feature… and ended up rewriting half your codebase?
You didn't break anything on purpose. You were careful. You tested. And yet something, somewhere, stopped working.
This is not bad luck. This is bad design.
And the principle being violated is called the Open-Closed Principle (OCP).

This chapter covers what OCP actually means, why touching existing code to add new behavior is always risky, how to build systems that grow without breaking, and the traps most developers fall into along the way.
1. The Problem: A Notification System That Keeps Growing
blocks.text: 1. The Problem: A Notification System That Keeps Growing

blocks.content: You are building a notification system for a project management tool. At launch, you only need one thing email notifications.
Simple enough:

Then your manager says "Users want SMS alerts too."
Fine. You crack open NotificationSender and add it:
And updateAlertServiceto handle both:
Then Slack integration gets requested. Then WhatsApp. Then push notifications.
Every single time you reopen the same class. You add another method. You add another else if. And every single time, you put everything that already works at risk.
1. Why This Hurts More Than You Think
blocks.text: 1. Why This Hurts More Than You Think

blocks.content: Bugs sneak in through the back door. You are editing working, tested, production code. A misplaced variable or a copy-paste slip can silently break email notifications while you were only trying to add Slack support.

Testing never ends. Every change forces you to retest everything not just the new channel. Did email still work after the Slack update? Did SMS break when you added WhatsApp? You can never be sure without running it all again.

The class becomes unreadable. One massive class handling five different notification channels, full of branching logic, is a nightmare for anyone new to the codebase. Nobody knows where one responsibility ends and another begins.
Growth becomes the enemy. The more notification types you add, the more fragile and bloated the class becomes. What started as 10 lines is now 200 and growing.
This constant reopening and rewriting of existing code is exactly what the Open-Closed Principle exists to prevent.
2. Introducing the Open-Closed Principle (OCP)
"Software entities should be open for extension, but closed for modification."
Let's break that down:
Open for Extension: When new requirements arrive like a new notification channel you should be able to add new behavior by writing new code, not rewriting old code.
Closed for Modification: Once a class is written, tested, and working, it should not need to be touched just because something new is being added.
Sounds impossible, right? How do you add new behavior without changing anything?
The answer is abstraction.

Instead of programming against concrete implementations, you program against interfaces. New behavior comes from new classes that implement the existing interface not from editing classes that already work.
The diagram below shows what an OCP-compliant notification system looks like. The AlertService depends on a NotificationChannel interface, and each concrete channel implements that interface.
Adding a new channel like WhatsAppNotification means creating one new class. Nothing existing is touched. Nothing existing can break.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-images/1778245771476-1bb6a4a1.png
Notice how AlertService only knows about the NotificationChannel interface. It has absolutely no idea whether it is sending an email, an SMS, a Slack message, or a WhatsApp alert.
Each concrete implementation plugs in freely and the core system never needs to change.
3. Why Does OCP Matter?
Before jumping into implementation, let's understand why this principle is actually worth the effort.
Safer to maintain. Adding new notification channels means writing new code, not editing old code. Your existing email and SMS logic stays untouched and trustworthy.
Scales without pain. Ten notification channels or twenty — it doesn't matter. Each one is its own isolated class. The core system never feels the weight of growth.
Fewer regressions. You cannot break what you don't touch. Since existing classes are never modified, already-working features stay working.
Test once, trust forever. New channels are tested in isolation. You don't need to rerun tests for email every time you add Slack support.
Reusable by design. A NotificationChannel interface that works in your project management tool today can plug straight into your CRM tomorrow.
Now let's build it.
4. Implementing OCP
Let's rebuild our NotificationSender the right way using abstraction to make it open for extension and closed for modification.
Step 1: Define an Interface
We create a NotificationChannel interface that sets the contract. Every notification type must implement a send method.
Step 2: Implement Concrete Channels
Each notification type gets its own class. Each class is self-contained and knows only about its own delivery logic.
Step 3: Refactor the Sender to Use the Abstraction
blocks.text: Step 3: Refactor the Sender to Use the Abstraction

blocks.content: NotificationSender now depends on the interface not on any concrete channel. No if-else. No switch. No reason to ever change this class again.
Step 4: Final Alert Service Implementation
AlertService simply passes the channel to the sender. It doesn't care which channel it is it just delegates.
Step 5: Usage
Now the client wants WhatsApp notifications? Push notifications? In-app alerts?
Create a new class that implements NotificationChannel. Implement its send method. Done.
NotificationSender never changes. AlertService never changes. The entire existing system stays exactly as it was closed for modification, open for whatever comes next.
5. Common Pitfalls While Applying OCP
OCP sounds clean in theory. In practice, these are the mistakes developers make most often.
Abstracting Everything Too Early

Not every class needs an interface. If your app sends notifications via email only and there's no real chance that changes building a full NotificationChannel abstraction is wasted effort. Premature abstraction creates complexity without delivering any real benefit. Apply OCP where change is likely, not where it's imaginable.
Thinking "Closed" Means Frozen

"Closed for modification" does not mean the class is untouchable forever. If there's a bug, fix it. If the logic needs refactoring for clarity, refactor it. OCP only applies to adding new behavior not to correcting mistakes or improving existing code.
Building Abstraction Layers Nobody Asked For

Four interfaces, three abstract classes, and two factory patterns just to send a message. This is abstraction for abstraction's sake and it makes the code harder to read, harder to debug, and harder to onboard new developers. Clarity is the goal. Abstraction is just a tool to get there.
Applying OCP Mechanically

Slapping interfaces onto everything without understanding why produces code that looks OCP-compliant but isn't actually more maintainable. Always ask what is likely to change here? Who benefits from this extension point? OCP without that thinking is just extra boilerplate.
Putting Extension Points in the Wrong Places

This is the most costly mistake. You build a beautifully flexible notification system — but hardcode the business rules that actually change every sprint. OCP only helps when you identify the right places to leave open. That instinct comes from understanding your domain, not just the principle.
6. Common Questions About OCP
"Does OCP mean I can never touch existing code?"

Not at all. Bugs get fixed. Code gets refactored. OCP simply means you shouldn't have to reopen working, tested code just to add something new. Extension through new classes not edits to old ones is the goal.
"Should I apply OCP to every class I write?"

No. Start simple. Apply OCP in areas where you genuinely anticipate variation payment methods, notification channels, report formats, third-party integrations. Stable, low-change code doesn't need it. Forcing OCP everywhere is just over-engineering with extra steps.
"Isn't creating a new class for every feature overkill?"

It feels that way at first. But compare it to the alternative a bloated class full of branching logic that breaks every time you breathe near it. A few extra focused classes is a small price for a system that stays clean, testable, and safe to extend for years.
